newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt to hang, jail militants for police killings.
newsitem.headline: Egypt to hang, jail militants for police killings.

text.p: Egyptian Moslem militants on Monday chanted in celebration as a Supreme State Security Court judge ratified death sentences for five of them and handed down jail terms to 19 others.

The men were among 32 in the trial which started in March on charges that included killing 10 policemen, some of them high-ranking officers, and 10 civilians near Abu Tig town, 345 km (215 miles) south of Cairo, in Assiut province.
The men kissed and embraced each other after Judge Salah Budur handed down the sentences.
Budur acquitted seven men, and police shot dead another defendant who was on the run after the start of the trial.

Prosecutors said the men belonged to the militant Gama'a al-Islamiya (Islamic Group) and had blasted buildings and shot at trains in southern Egypt between 1993 to 1994. They were also charged with illegally possessing weapons.
The militants waved copies of the Koran at television cameras and photographers from behind the bars of the courtroom cage where defendants are kept during the trial.
They carried on their shoulders one of their co-defendants who was shrouded in white cloth according to Islamic burial rituals to symbolise the impending death sentences.

"I'm happy. I have won martyrdom. I am not afraid of execution. How can anyone be unhappy if they are going to heaven," said Mostafa Mohammed Mahmoud Issa, 26, after Budur had ratified his sentence of death by hanging.
"We know this judge is a criminal. I am innocent and he (Budur) himself said the confessions were invalid because they were made under torture," Issa told Reuters.
A woman named Shaima, whose brother el-Nimeri Ramadan Sayyed Hassan, 20, will also hang, collapsed and sobbed in the courtroom.
"He's been sentenced to death without any proof. If they have any proof let them show it. God will deal with you Salah Budur," she screamed.

Budur gave five of the men life sentences, four were sentenced to 15 years, nine were given 10 years and one man was sentenced to five years in prison. All the jail terms are accompanied by hard labour.
Seven of the men are on the run including two who were sentenced to death.
Defence lawyer Sa'ad Hasaballah said he would appeal the sentences because some of the convicted men were in Cairo when the killings took place in Abu Tig.

"Remember me in your prayers, brother. Don't say we have lost a martyr," the men chanted. "The youth of the Islamic revival is encroaching. We don't hesitate, our fire is strong and we are the challengers."
Budur had passed the execution terms last month but they had to be sent to the Grand Mufti, Egypt's highest spiritual adviser, for approval.
More than 1,000 people, mainly militants and policemen, have been killed in Egypt since militant groups took up arms against the government in 1992.
Egypt has executed at least 53 of the 76 people it has sentenced to death since then.
